newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel says NATO should have expansion timetable.
newsitem.headline: Havel says NATO should have expansion timetable.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel pledged his support on Monday for Romania's bid to join NATO and said the alliance should work out a timetable for admitting all suitable applicant countries.

Havel, whose country is a leading candidate to be among the first wave of new NATO members, told a briefing with visiting Romanian President Emil Constantinescu that the alliance should be open to all democratic states in the region.
"I assured Mr President that the Czech Republic shows solidarity with Romanian efforts to become a member of this alliance," Havel said.

Constantinescu wants Romania to be among the first new members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), which will invite chosen countries for further talks on joining after a Madrid summit in July.
The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are the leading contenders but Romania, whose bid to join NATO is winning widespread Western support, and Slovenia are also under discussion.

"Romania is fully prepared to enter in the first wave," Constantinescu said. "My friends from the West have advised me to react in the other way and ask what is the argument for Romania not being in the first wave," he added.
However, Havel did not explicitly endorse Bucharest's bid to be among the first new members but said that NATO enlargement was not a competition.
"Despite the fact that we know that the alliance can hardly, for various reasons, suddenly take in all applicants, there must be a certain sequence.
"Despite that (NATO) should give certainty to all in the spirit of the Washington agreement, give hope to everybody and explain the logic of the potential schedule of its enlargement," Havel said.
"The point is for NATO to be an alliance open to all democratic countries in the Euro-Atlantic area," he said.
Havel, a former dissident playwright, said there should be no discrimination against any democracy seeking to join NATO.

The eastward expansion of the alliance is bitterly opposed by Moscow, which sees it as a threat to its national security, and will be the key topic when Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin meet in a summit in Helsinki later this month.
Constantinescu, who has pledged tough reforms since his centrists ousted foamier communists in elections last year, said expansion was no threat.
"NATO should be a symbol of cooperation and not a symbol of something which is opposed to any other country," he said.

The enlargement debate has a special significance in Prague as Slovakia, which became independent in 1993 when Czehoslovakia split, is seen unlikely to be invited at the same time as the Czechs after criticism by the United States and European Union of the pace of democratic reform there.

Czech Deputy Foreign Minister Karel Kovanda said last week after a seminar on the future of the alliance's Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme that the initiative should be expanded as a forum for cooperation between NATO members and others.

But Czech officials have said more needs to be done at home to explain to the Czech people what NATO membership would entail. A January opinion poll showed just 37 percent of Czechs favoured membership while 32 percent were against.
